questions.stem: A 5-month-old has tachypnea, irritability, and decreased feeding after a viral illness. Which finding most strongly suggests poor systemic perfusion?

options.A: Cool extremities with delayed capillary refill

questions.rationale: Cool extremities and delayed capillary refill indicate impaired systemic perfusion and low cardiac output.

option_explanations.A: Correct. These are direct bedside perfusion findings.
option_explanations.D: Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude low cardiac output.

questions.board_pearl: Cardiac output failure can be present even when oxygen saturation is normal.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old with suspected myocarditis has frequent palpitations, but the admission ECG is normal. Which test best addresses the possibility of intermittent arrhythmia?

options.A: Continuous telemetry or ambulatory ECG monitoring

questions.rationale: Intermittent arrhythmias may not be captured on a single ECG; continuous or ambulatory monitoring improves detection.

option_explanations.A: Correct. This directly tests the suspected intermittent rhythm problem.
option_explanations.C: May identify a contributor but not the rhythm.

questions.board_pearl: A normal resting ECG is a snapshot, not a rhythm guarantee.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has chest pain, dyspnea, elevated troponin, and mild LV dysfunction. He also has severe hypertension and retinal changes consistent with hypertensive emergency. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Consider pressure-related myocardial injury and do not assume myocarditis solely from troponin elevation
options.C: Ignore the blood pressure because myocarditis causes all LV dysfunction

questions.rationale: Severe hypertension can cause myocardial injury and dysfunction; the alternative mechanism must be integrated into the differential.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The clinical context provides another cause of myocardial injury.
option_explanations.C: Hypertensive emergency is a major care-changing finding.
option_explanations.D: The data do not establish isolated pericarditis.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis is a diagnosis of integration, not a synonym for elevated troponin.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with myocarditis has moderate LV dysfunction and is admitted. Which monitoring strategy is most appropriate in the early phase?

options.A: Continuous rhythm monitoring with serial hemodynamic assessment
options.C: No monitoring if the child is awake

questions.rationale: Acute myocarditis can deteriorate through pump failure or arrhythmia, so early continuous rhythm and close hemodynamic monitoring are appropriate.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It addresses both major acute hazards.
option_explanations.C: Awake status does not eliminate risk.
option_explanations.D: Pulse oximetry cannot detect low output or arrhythmia reliably.

questions.board_pearl: Early myocarditis monitoring must watch both circulation and rhythm.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with probable myocarditis has CMR showing edema but no late gadolinium enhancement. Which interpretation is best?

options.A: The findings may still support acute inflammation; CMR features should be integrated rather than reduced to one sequence
options.C: The patient must have coronary infarction
options.D: CMR is invalid if EF is normal

questions.rationale: Modern CMR diagnosis incorporates multiple tissue markers; absence of one feature does not automatically negate other evidence of myocardial inflammation.

option_explanations.C: No ischemic territorial pattern is described.
option_explanations.D: CMR remains useful with preserved EF.
option_explanations.E: Follow-up depends on the overall clinical syndrome.

questions.board_pearl: Do not turn CMR into a single-feature yes/no test.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with fulminant myocarditis is on escalating support. Which sign suggests that waiting longer before transfer for advanced support could be dangerous?

options.A: Progressive hepatic and renal dysfunction from low output

questions.rationale: Progressive end-organ dysfunction means inadequate perfusion is already causing injury and should accelerate advanced-support decisions.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Organ injury is a late and dangerous sign of persistent shock.

questions.board_pearl: Do not wait for cardiac arrest to decide that conventional support has failed.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with fever and tachycardia has a new gallop, hepatomegaly, elevated BNP, and depressed LV function. Which diagnosis is least adequate as a stand-alone explanation?
questions.rationale: A simple URI cannot explain the objective signs of heart failure and ventricular dysfunction.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It is an insufficient explanation for the cardiac findings.
option_explanations.B: Fits the postviral myocardial dysfunction pattern.

questions.board_pearl: When objective cardiac findings appear, stop explaining everything with the antecedent viral illness.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old has recurrent episodes of clinically confirmed myocarditis separated by complete recovery. Which next consideration becomes more important than in a single isolated episode?

options.A: Evaluation for underlying genetic or immune predisposition
options.B: Assuming every recurrence is identical viral infection

questions.rationale: Recurrent myocarditis should raise concern for an underlying predisposition, including genetic cardiomyopathy or immune mechanisms, and merits specialist evaluation.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Recurrence changes the etiologic differential.
option_explanations.B: Repeated identical infection should not be assumed.
option_explanations.E: Recurrent disease increases the need for careful cardiac assessment.

questions.board_pearl: Recurrent myocarditis is a clue to look beyond a one-time viral trigger.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with myocarditis has right ventricular as well as left ventricular dysfunction. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Biventricular involvement indicates more extensive myocardial dysfunction and may increase severity concern
options.C: Only LV function matters in prognosis
options.E: The finding is always benign in children

questions.rationale: Myocarditis can affect both ventricles; RV dysfunction can mark more severe disease and should heighten clinical concern.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Biventricular failure represents broader pump involvement.
option_explanations.C: RV performance can be clinically important.
option_explanations.D: PE is one differential but not proven by RV dysfunction alone.

questions.board_pearl: Assess both ventricles; myocarditis is not an LV-only disease.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has normalized symptoms and EF after myocarditis but still has frequent ventricular ectopy during exercise testing. What is the best recommendation?

options.A: Defer competitive sports and continue cardiology evaluation
options.B: Clear immediately because EF is normal
options.C: Ignore ectopy if troponin is normal
options.D: Use exercise as treatment for the ectopy
options.E: No further rhythm assessment is needed

questions.rationale: Exercise-associated ventricular ectopy indicates residual electrical risk and is incompatible with routine sports clearance.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Rhythm risk overrides symptom/EF normalization.
option_explanations.C: Troponin does not negate arrhythmic risk.
option_explanations.D: Exercise is not treatment for potentially dangerous ectopy.

questions.board_pearl: The last abnormal recovery domain can determine clearance—even when all the others have normalized.
